"Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah — flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father has revealed it." The revelation was to Peter's heart and to Peter's spirit, long before it ever came to his head, and out of that revelation of the inner working of the Spirit of God, Peter made his confession: "Thou art the Christ." Jesus then goes on and says, "Your name shall no longer be called Peter — it shall be called the Rock, for upon this rock I am going to build my church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it." What rock, Peter? No, no — Peter was a crumbling stone, who crumbled at the words of a little girl in Pilate's judgment hall, until he was filled with the Spirit of God. What Jesus is saying is that he is going to build his church upon men and women like you, Peter, who receive a revelation from God in their spirit, not in their heads. I'm not talking about hearing voices — I'm talking about our spirits being so in tune with the Spirit of God that when he says move right, we move right. When he says move left, we move left; when he says stop, we stop — not in the head, I'm not talking about voices, I'm talking about being led by the Spirit of God because we walk hand in hand with him, the Son. That's what faith is. The Walk of Faith So let me define faith for you. I believe faith is an attribute of the heart, evidenced in obedience — obedience to what God the Holy Spirit says through his written word, which speaks to our spirits, dividing the soul from the spirit and allowing us to be free to follow what the Spirit of God says. Obedience to the small, inner voice of his Spirit speaking to our spirits, amidst all the clamor of the other voices we hear in our minds. Obedience when he convicts us, and we respond by seeking again forgiveness and cleansing. Evidenced in obedience to everything the Spirit of God wants to do in us. One of the characteristics Jesus named in the Sermon on the Mount is, "Blessed is the meek man." We have this false understanding that meekness is equivalent to weakness, but Jesus was called meek — the word meek literally means teachable, moldable, pliable. We sing songs about being clay in the potter's hand — clay in the potter's hand yields to every pressure of the potter's fingers; if there are lumps, he takes them out, he keeps working on it. I want to be such clay in the hands of my Lord that when he squeezes, there is the imprint of his thumb marks upon me. That is what faith is: allowing him to do his work, and having such a meek, pliable, teachable spirit that as he molds me, I am pliable, and he molds me. That is what the work of faith is — nothing to do with the head, everything to do with the heart. Allowing God to speak, to breathe, to put his finger into our spirit and mold us, and we yield in obedience to every little pressure of the finger of God, or every little word from the mouth of God. We yield because our spirits are in tune with him. That is what faith is — the faith that pleases God, the faith that enables us to walk the walk of faith. So let me repeat: faith is an attribute of the heart, evidenced in obedience — evidenced in obedience. It's the finger of God in the hearts of men and women, moving them to do his will. I made a decision, when I came to understand this a few years ago, that I was going to hold his hand, to know him as Abba, Father. My commitment, day by day, is that I am holding my Father's hand. I do not know where he's going to lead me tomorrow — six weeks ago I did not know he was going to lead me to the departure of a Baptist church. I'm thrilled and delighted he brought me here — this is sweet time, this is honey time. This is the kind of pleasure my earthly father periodically gave me when he took me to the sweet shop. My heavenly Father has brought me to a sweet shop with you people, and I delight in the sweet shop of God. But I've learned, long ago, in my walk, that if I go to the sweet shop often, I often have to go to the dentist's shop too — and sometimes my heavenly Father takes me to the dentist's shop. But I'm holding his hand, because I know the dentist's shop is good for me. That's what the walk of faith is. So committed to holding my Father's hand, trusting him to lead — I do not know where he'll lead me tomorrow, but I know he holds tomorrow. I want to climb to that mountaintop, but I know he's going to probably have to take me through a valley to get there. The walk of faith is not a walk in beds of roses, in lullaby fields full of daffodils. The walk of faith often takes us through the sloughs of despondency, pain, and suffering. I do not believe in a Christianity that is all victory and happiness and glory, glory, hallelujah — praise God, it's going to be one day — but if my Savior was perfected through his suffering, why should I ask for less? But the walk of faith, with its sweet shops and its dentist's shop, its valleys and its mountains, comes to those who are committed to holding the hand of the Father. My earthly father was not a Christian, but he was a very good father. I think, if I was a little child holding his hand and somebody bounced a ball into the road, I would let go of my father's hand and go chasing after the little ball — I did it often, and I do that as a Christian sometimes too. I let go of my Father's hand and run after the temptations of Satan. But just as my earthly father would never allow me to go out into the road while a ten-ton truck was coming, so my heavenly Father has promised to keep me — he gathers me in by the work of the Spirit and pulls me back before I fall into danger. That's the walk of faith. And I've learned, long ago, that I'm foolish to let go of his hand. Faith, my brothers and sisters, is not a commitment to believe in things, and to do things, and to believe in a hope, or a presumption. Faith is a commitment to hold the Father's hand, and allow him to lead where he will. There is a verse of Scripture I want to conclude with — I gave you a verse in the King James a moment ago that does not say what the actual Greek says; there are many verses like that. This one is found in Galatians, a verse you all know very well, and I'm going to suggest to you that, without you realizing it, you'll probably find it too has a different translation from what the Greek says — and believe me, I'm not a Greek scholar. I did two years of studying Greek, but I have learned how to use Strong's Concordance with Greek, and I do know that Greek, being a very classical language, means what it says. Look with me, please, at Galatians chapter 2, verse 20. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who gave himself for me. Can you say that this morning — is that true? "And the life which I now live in the flesh I live" — many of your Bibles are going to say, "by faith in the Son of God, who gave himself for me." Is that true? Is that what your Bible says? If you've got the King James Version, it does not say that — and the King James Version, this time, is correct. The King James Version says, "I live by the faith of the Son of God, who gave himself for me." Now, think about it — they are two radically different things. Do I live this life by faith in him, or by his faith in me? The Greek, let me assure you, says, "I live this life by his faith, operative in me." I live this life because he — my Lord, my King — is the one who speaks into me, who breathes into me, who puts his finger into me and prompts me to move this way and that. And if I am a meek man, if my spirit is teachable and moldable, he will produce in me what he wants to do — just as he did in Abraham, just as he did in Rahab the harlot, just as he did in the people of the Old Testament, just as he did with five young men who went to Ecuador in 1957 and died on the banks of the Curaray River. All of North America wept for these brilliant young American men who died — "How is God in this? What is God doing?" they all cried. But ten years later we saw a barrier broken down to the Auca Indians that had stood for centuries, so that tens of thousands of them became believers in Christ, because five men died on the banks of the Curaray River. Did Jesus intend and plan for them to die? I suggest to you: yes — by faith these five young men died, part of God's will, so that God would open a breach in the walls that had trapped the Auca Indians for centuries. That is how God operates. So when I see valleys and despair, I ask myself: are you walking right now in the will of God? Are you walking in faith? That's what it means to be a man of faith, walking the life of faith, walking in obedience to it. My prayer for myself is that I will continue to walk this life holding his hand, being led by him. I'm not asking to hear voices, but I am certainly asking for my spirit to be entwined with his, so that his Spirit can mold me, prompt me, lead me, guide me. I pray that may be true for you as well. Let's pray. Father, thank you for this word. I pray that you will speak to each of our spirits. Your word is sharper than any two-edged sword — it divides the soul from the spirit, the natural man from the spiritual. So we ask, Lord, that by your spoken word, even the still, small voice to us, you will make us men and women who work and walk and live in faith that pleases you. I ask this in Jesus's name. Amen.
